newsitem.title: CHINA: China says yuan not to slide in 1997, reserves up.
newsitem.headline: China says yuan not to slide in 1997, reserves up.

text.p: China's central bank will not bow to pressure from exporters to allow the yuan to depreciate and expects foreign exchange reserves to swell by at least $20 billion this year, officials said on Wednesday.

The central People's Bank of China will not allow the yuan to rise significantly in 1997, nor will it bow to pressure from exporters to depress the domestic currency, the Xinhua news agency quoted an official of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE) as saying.
"If the central bank can buy foreign exchange at a cheaper price, why should it pay a higher price?" it quoted the official as saying.
"Exporters should improve their competitiveness through their own efforts."
China's yuan would remain under pressure to appreciate this year, he said.
"All the measurable factors foretell the further expansion of our reserves and an oversupply of foreign exchange, leaving the yuan under pressure to gain more ground," he said.

Since Beijing devalued the yuan in January 1994 to 8.7 to the dollar from 5.7, it has appreciated steadily. It gained nearly 0.3 percent against the dollar last year, after rising by 1.5 percent in 1995 and 2.9 percent in 1994, he said.
China's foreign exchange reserves have grown sharply to $105 billion at the end of 1996, up $31.5 billion from the beginning of that year.
The official said a trade surplus expected this year coupled with a further rise in direct foreign investment would put upward pressure on the yuan.

"The yuan will remain solid unless basic construction overheats and imports run out of control," Tao Liming, deputy director of the International Finance Research Institute under the Bank of China, told Xinhua.
He expected to see the yuan in short supply this year as the central bank continued a moderately tight monetary policy.
"Overall, the forces pushing up the value of the local currency still exist this year and I don't see any signs for it to depreciate in a foreseeable timeframe," Tao said.
He said he expected foreign exchange reserves to grow by about $20 billion in 1997.
He said the central bank would continue to buy hard currencies despite criticism that the rapidly expanding reserves were partly to blame for recent inflationary pressures.
"There is no way for the central bank to avoid the bad effects of a consolidating exchange rate and an enormous foreign exchange reserve at the same time," Tao said.
"From a realistic point of view, the central bank will opt for a relatively stable exchange rate of the yuan and let the currency reserves grow," he said.
However, a second SAFE official warned China's emphasis on the stability of the yuan could damage the economy.
"The market will decide the value of the yuan," he said. "Why should we let overseas speculators take advantage of our promise to keep it stable?"
The yuan closed at 8.2956 to the dollar on Wednesday in Shanghai against Tuesday's 8.2955.
